reports.title: Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts
reports.description: The overarching accounting framework Statistics Canada operates under for macroeconomic statistics -- the umbrella that the quarterly income-and-expenditure accounts (statcan-national-accounts, IMDB record 1901), monthly GDP by industry (statcan-gdp-monthly), the Supply and Use Tables (statcan-sut) and the National Balance Sheet Accounts all sit inside, per the User Guide's own chapter structure and per record 1901's language describing the annual benchmarks as arising 'through the construction of annual supply and use tables' within this system. Minted as a node in its own right 2026-08-08 because two federal fiscal-transfer regulations (SOR/2007-303, both the Equalization and Territorial Formula Financing divisions) name the framework itself -- not a specific release -- as the thing a statutory wage/salary term is 'determined... for the purpose of': 'as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of its System of Macroeconomic Accounts'. Thomas's ruling (2026-08-08, Open-Questions-2026-08-08-sweep.docx Q1): frameworks and legislative instruments a regulation is built on are worth a node even with no cadence of their own -- 'its sole role is broadcasting and that needs represented.' No releases_per_year: this is an evergreen framework, not a periodic release, the same shape as the one-off foundational instruments already in the corpus.

reports.title: Quarterly Survey of Financial Statements (QSFS)
reports.description: Quarterly survey (IMDB record 2501) of the financial position and performance of Canadian incorporated businesses, collected roughly 30 days after the end of each quarter. Named in record 1901's 'Data sources' list among the quarterly national accounts' 'more notable sources', named again in record 1901's 'Estimation' section as one of the sub-annual surveys whose movements are applied to annual benchmarks, and named a third time in the monthly GDP by industry source table as the input behind financial intermediation and insurance industry output. Minted 2026-08-09 (sweep session, Tier-2 item #15), closing a `no-node-yet` lead that had already identified the record number but not confirmed its own publication facts.
reports.cadence_note: Statistics Canada's own record 2501: 'Frequency: Quarterly'; collection occurs approximately 30 days after quarter-end.

reports.title: Retail Commodity Survey (RCS)
reports.description: Statistics Canada's own IMDB record 2008 names this the Retail Commodity Survey (RCS), a monthly survey of retail commodity sales in Canada by outlet type, which 'produces more detailed quarterly estimates' at the commodity level. Named in record 1901's 'Data sources' list as one of the quarterly national accounts' 'more notable sources' under the name 'Quarterly Retail Commodity Survey', and appearing repeatedly in the monthly GDP by industry source table alongside the CPI for retail-trade industries as 'Retail commodity survey, Record no. 2008'. NAME DISCREPANCY, recorded rather than resolved: both citing documents call it the 'Quarterly Retail Commodity Survey,' but the survey's own current IMDB record names it the 'Retail Commodity Survey' with a monthly base frequency and quarterly commodity-level detail. Whether this reflects a historical rename (older Daily articles from 1999-2012 do use the 'Quarterly Retail Commodity Survey' name) or the citing documents using an informal name for the quarterly detail specifically is not adjudicated here. Minted 2026-08-09 (sweep session, Tier-2 item #15) under the record's own current title.
reports.cadence_note: Record 2008's own current page: 'Frequency: Monthly', with quarterly commodity-level detail as a secondary tier — the same shape as several ECB series this corpus already treats as one node with a headline cadence rather than two.

dependencies.basis: The monthly program publishes an industry-by-industry source table, 'National monthly gross domestic product by industry, summary of Methods and data sources', which names the CPI by title and by IMDB record number as the deflator for the industries it applies to — 27 separate rows. Representative row, NAICS 441 Motor vehicle and parts dealers, under 'Gross output': 'Deflated sales and margins, Retail trade survey (monthly), Record no. 2406, Consumer price indexes adjusted for sales tax changes, Record no. 2301, Retail commodity survey, Record no. 2008, Retail trade survey (annual), Record no. 2422.' Record 2301 is the Consumer Price Index. `uses_data_from` rather than `methodology_depends_on` because the document's own column heading classifies it as a data source and the index values are the divisor, not a method the program borrows — the CPI's published numbers are an input.

Record 1301's 'Data sources' section names the release outright: 'For example, data from the Monthly Survey of Manufacturing are used for most (but not all) manufacturing industries. Data from the Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours (SEPH) are used for many service industries.' The industry source table corroborates it at release level in 37 rows, typically as 'Number of employees, Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours, Record no. 2612' — record 2612 being SEPH.

Record 1901 — the same IMDB record this node's own url points at — names SEPH twice. Under 'Data sources': 'Some of the more notable sources include: the Quarterly Survey of Financial Statements, the monthly Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours, the Quarterly Retail Commodity Survey, annual business surveys, banking information, Government Finance Statistics, the balance of payments statistics, and the T4 remuneration file from the Canada Revenue Agency.' Under 'Estimation': 'The sub-annual estimates are generated by applying the movements of sub-annual surveys such as the Quarterly Survey of Financial Statements, the Monthly Survey of Manufacturing and the monthly Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours to the benchmark estimates.' Named release, stated use, publisher's own methodology record.

Record 1901's 'Estimation' section: 'The sub-annual estimates are generated by applying the movements of sub-annual surveys such as the Quarterly Survey of Financial Statements, the Monthly Survey of Manufacturing and the monthly Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours to the benchmark estimates.' `statcan-msm` already exists as a corpus node (manufacturing-and-classifications.json, IMDB record 2101), closing the node-availability blocker this entry was filed under.

Record 1901's 'Data sources' list: 'Some of the more notable sources include: the Quarterly Survey of Financial Statements...' and the 'Estimation' section names it again as a sub-annual movement source. `statcan-qsfs` minted this session (IMDB record 2501, quarterly).
The monthly GDP by industry source table names the input behind financial intermediation and insurance output: 'Quarterly survey of financial statements, Record no. 2501.'

Record 1901's 'Data sources' list names 'the Quarterly Retail Commodity Survey' among 'the more notable sources' for the quarterly accounts. `statcan-rcs` minted this session under its current IMDB title (record 2008) — see the node's own description for the name discrepancy this citation surfaced.
The monthly GDP by industry source table names 'Retail commodity survey, Record no. 2008' repeatedly alongside the CPI for retail-trade industries.

_dropped.why: Deleted, not merely unevidenced. This was a seed edge whose basis asserted that 'the quarterly expenditure-based accounts are reconciled against the monthly by-industry GDP estimates'. Both programs' IMDB records were read in full and neither states it, and the quarterly record refutes it by enumeration: record 1901's 'Estimation' section lists what the sub-annual quarterly estimates are built from — 'the Quarterly Survey of Financial Statements, the Monthly Survey of Manufacturing and the monthly Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours' applied to annual benchmarks — and monthly GDP by industry is not among them, nor does it appear in the record's 'Data sources' list. Record 1301 points the anchoring the other way: 'The monthly estimates are benchmarked to annually chained Fisher volume indexes of GDP obtained from the constant-price supply and use tables', and 'GDP by industry depends on the Supply and Use tables to which it is anchored.' The only relation the two documents assert between the quarterly and monthly measures is comparability, not dependency: 'This makes the monthly GDP by industry estimates more comparable with the expenditure-based GDP data, which are chained quarterly.' Both series hang off the same annual Supply and Use benchmark; neither reads the other. An external assistant returned this edge as DOCUMENTED, quoting 'the final step in the production of the monthly real GDP by industry estimates is their ongoing reconciliation with the quarterly estimates' — which describes the monthly depending on the quarterly, the reverse of the edge it was offered for, and which it flagged and then overrode. That string does not occur in the 2021 summary of methods and data sources ('reconcil' returns zero occurrences there); it was not searched for in Catalogue 15-547-X, which was not opened. Even taken at face value the quote supports the reverse edge, and the reverse edge is contradicted by record 1301's own account of what the monthly estimates are benchmarked to.

_dropped.edge: statcan-gdp-monthly -> (Supply, Use and Input-Output Tables, IMDB record 1401)
_dropped.why: RESOLVED IN THE SAME SESSION — the node was built as `statcan-sut` and both edges taken; see research/statcan-supply-use-tables.json. Kept as a note rather than deleted because the reasoning below is what justified building it, and reclassified from `no-node-yet` so it stops being counted as an outstanding lead. Original entry follows. The strongest documented dependency of the monthly GDP by industry programme has nowhere to point. Record 1301 states it three ways: 'The monthly estimates are benchmarked to annually chained Fisher volume indexes of GDP obtained from the constant-price supply and use tables'; 'GDP by industry depends on the Supply and Use tables to which it is anchored'; and, in the programme description, 'The GDP by industry measures provide an alternate dimension that supplements the income and expenditure-based GDP estimates, and constitute an extension (on a monthly basis) of the Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts Supply and Use Tables (SUT).' The SUT is a distinct statistical programme with its own IMDB record (1401), annual, published about two and a half years after the reference year. It is also the shared benchmark that the quarterly income and expenditure accounts run off — record 1901: 'The annual benchmarks for GDP by the income approach and by the expenditure approach are generated through the construction of annual supply and use tables which balance the supply of each product in the economy against its use.' So one node buys two documented edges and makes the actual shape of the Canadian accounts visible: a common annual benchmark with a monthly and a quarterly projection hanging off it, rather than the two projections citing each other. Highest-value single node available in this cluster.

SEARCHED AND NOT FOUND — reclassified from `deferred` after a second pass looked for a confirming document and returned nothing. The strings 'Labour Force Survey', 'LFS', 'record 3701', 'record no. 3701' and 'average weekly earnings' near 'Labour Force' were searched across the 1301 methods document and the main IMDB record for 1301, and no correctly-numbered citation and no second document stating that the monthly GDP by industry programme uses Labour Force Survey data was located. So this is now an answer rather than a lead: on the public record the single mis-numbered mention is the only reference that exists. Original reasoning follows, and still holds. Named once and only once in the industry source table, and the citation is internally wrong, so it is not being taken on this document alone. The row reads 'Revenues declared on the Goods and Services Tax remittance form, Canada Revenue Agency. Average weekly earnings, Labour Force Survey, Record no. 3401, and Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours, Record no. 2612'. IMDB record 3401 is the Field Crop Reporting Series, not the Labour Force Survey — the LFS is record 3701, which is the record this project's statcan-lfs node points at. The release is named in words, which is what the standard asks for, but a single occurrence carrying a record number that resolves to an unrelated agriculture survey is thin evidence, and 'average weekly earnings' is SEPH's headline output rather than the LFS's. Worth one confirming document; not worth an edge yet. Recorded also as a corpus fact: a StatCan methodology document miscites a StatCan record number, so record numbers in these tables are corroboration and not proof.

_dropped.edge: statcan-hfce and statcan-national-accounts are the same IMDB record
_dropped.why: Surfaced while checking the deflation edge, and it is a curation problem rather than an evidence one. statcan-national-accounts points at https://www.statcan.gc.ca/en/survey/business/1901 and statcan-hfce points at https://www23.statcan.gc.ca/imdb/p2SV.pl?Function=getSurvey&SDDS=1901 — the same statistical programme, record 1901, 'National Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by Income and by Expenditure Accounts'. Household final consumption expenditure is a series inside that release, not a separate release, and the loader's duplicate detection cannot see this because the ids differ. It matters for two reasons. First, authority: the CPI's documented dependency on its basket weights lands on statcan-hfce (calculated_from, weight 1.0) while the release that publishes HFCE sits at a tenth position, so rank that belongs to one programme is split across two nodes. Second, it is the within-system-structure question from REPORTS.md in a new and sharper form — bea-gdp -> bea-pce is one release named as a component of another, whereas this is one release entered twice under different names. The honest options are to merge, or to keep the finer node and say in the data model that a node may be a named series within a release. Not resolved here, because both options move authority and the call is not a research one. Worth settling in the same pass as the bea-gdp -> bea-pce decision, since one answer should cover both.

_dropped.edge: statcan-national-accounts -> statcan-cpi (deflation) — retained as implied, not dropped
_dropped.why: Recorded here so the reasoning sits with the rest of the slice; the edge itself is live in dependencies.ts marked `implied`. The quarterly accounts' own guide describes deflation and names the CPI, but as an illustration of what a price index is rather than as a statement of what deflates what — User Guide: Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts ch. 5 §5.5: 'For example, the Consumer Price Index does precisely that for various classes of consumer products.' Record 1901 says only that 'certain series (mainly expenditure series) are deflated (presented in real terms)'. The monthly by-industry programme, by contrast, cites the CPI by name and record number for 27 industries. The dependency is almost certainly identical in both programmes and only one of them discloses it at release level, which is the pattern REPORTS.md already records for municipalities: where the graph looks uneven, suspect disclosure before reality. The candidate closing document is Catalogue 15F0077G, 'A guide to deflating the input-output accounts: sources and methods', cited by record 1301 for the double-deflation method and not opened this pass.
